extracted.intended_audience: employers who use H-1B/H-1B1/E-3 and PERM programs, immigration attorneys, HR professionals, labor economists, regulatory analysts, and public commenters on the NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory analysis and methodological guidance for revising prevailing wage computations for H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM programs, including proposed percentile structure, cost/transfer estimation methods, data sources, and an alternative experience-benchmarking approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory alignment: four wage levels commensurate with experience/education/supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department concluded that the existing wage levels were not adequately aligned with the statutory requirement under 8 U.S.C. 1182(p)(4) to provide four wage levels commensurate with experience, education, and level of supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble explains prior methodology relied on outdated percentile thresholds (approx. 17th, 34th, 50th, 67th) and failed to reflect labor market conditions, enabling underpayment of alien workers relative to U.S. counterparts. Any new methodology must implement four levels that satisfy the statutory commensurability standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed percentile structure for prevailing wage levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend §656.40(b) to codify four prevailing wage levels at approximately the 34th, 52nd, 70th, and 88th percentiles (Levels I–IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level I adjusted from 17th to 34th percentile; Level IV from ~67th to ~88th. Level II and III computed 'by dividing by three the difference between Levels I and IV' per INA formula, yielding approx. 52nd and 70th percentiles. The Department selected these percentiles as the proposed balanced approach but solicits comments and considered alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of BLS OEWS data to determine prevailing wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will use the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) survey wage data to establish prevailing wages in the H-1B, H-1B1, and E-3 visa classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisions add that determinations will be made by the OFLC NPC consistent with §656.40(b)(2). Where OEWS percentiles are available for a SOC/area combination, they form the basis for prevailing wage computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear interpolation between reported OEWS percentiles to estimate proposed percentiles
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate wages at the new 34th, 52nd, 70th, and 88th percentiles, the Department linearly interpolated between OEWS-reported percentiles (10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th) for each SOC code and geographic area combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear interpolation is used when the OEWS does not directly report the exact percentile; this is the methodology for generating estimated wages at the proposed percentile targets for each occupation/area cell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling unmatched certifications and missing OEWS percentiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Some certifications cannot be matched to a new prevailing wage level due to unreleasable wages or missing OEWS percentiles; for these, estimate wage impacts by applying average wage impact per cohort and fiscal year to all workers associated with unmatched certifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First calculate the average wage impact per worker for the relevant cohort and fiscal year (from matched data), then apply that average to unmatched certifications to produce estimated annual wage impacts; add these to directly calculated impacts from matched certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and affected-entity counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of affected entities is calculated using OFLC performance data from FYs 2020-2025; LCA and OEWS data used to estimate wage impacts and percent of positions above new policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use OFLC performance data throughout the analysis to estimate costs and transfers. A merged OEWS-LCA dataset is used for certain proxy calculations; where full LCA data differ, calculated percentages serve as proxies for broader dataset estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation of rule familiarization costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule familiarization cost estimated by multiplying the average number of unique employers requesting H-1B and PERM certifications by the estimated review time (1 hour) and the hourly fully-loaded compensation rate for Human Resources Specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: average unique employers = 89,855; review time = 1 hour; fully-loaded HR specialist rate = $60.94 results in an initial first-year cost of $5.17 million. Continuing annual costs use the number of new unique employers (e.g., 42,896) to compute ongoing yearly familiarization costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation rate assumptions (fully-loaded wage calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use BLS mean hourly wage for private sector Human Resources Specialists ($38.33) and adjust to total compensation using a 42% fringe benefits rate and a 17% overhead rate, yielding a fully-loaded hourly wage of $60.94.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fringe benefits based on Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (paid leave, supplemental pay, insurance, retirement, legally required benefits). Overhead and fringe increase with wages; those percentages are applied uniformly in cost calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory analysis timeframe and discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiable impacts are analyzed over a 10-year period (2026–2035) and expressed in 2024 dollars; discount rates of 3% and 7% are used consistent with OMB Circular A-4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on incremental consequences of finalizing the rule above the analytic baseline. Unless noted, same methods/inputs are used across transfers, benefits, and costs; present both undiscounted annual averages and annualized figures at both discount rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of transfer payments per Circular A-4
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer payments are considered payments from one group to another that do not affect total resources available to society (or, if they do, only via uncaptured incentive effects). The regulatory impact analysis focuses on costs and transfer payments attributable exclusively to the new requirements in the NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify transfers where possible (e.g., employer wage payments rising to new prevailing wage), and separate quantifiable transfers from non-quantifiable transfer impacts; discuss but do not quantify transfers that are expected to be de minimis (e.g., some PERM cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort modeling of H-1B certifications and overlapping impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify certifications into cohorts by employment length (less than one year; one to two years; two to three years) and model annual wage impacts for each cohort, accounting for overlapping cohorts as new certifications enter each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transition pattern: Year 1 affects only new certifications; Year 2 affects new plus continuing approvals from Year 1; Year 3 includes new and continuing from prior two years. Because multi-year certifications extend beyond three-year horizons and new certifications continue each year, steady state is reached only after several years (analysis notes steadystate roughly by Year 6 or about Year 8 depending on cohort assumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage-change assumption for impacted workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that wages of workers already above the new prevailing wage remain unchanged, while those below the new prevailing wage are raised to exactly the new prevailing wage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delivers an upper-bound estimate on wage transfers because it assumes full upward adjustment for all below-threshold workers. Department notes it is unlikely the full increase would apply to the majority of workers currently earning below the new prevailing wage (~80%). Example: yields estimated annual wage transfer of approx. $14,000 per worker under these assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment for approvals based on OEWS vs alternative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate that 93.5% of workers associated with H-1B, H-1B1, and E-3 certifications had prevailing wages based on OEWS in FY 2024; to estimate OEWS-based approvals, multiply DHS approvals by 93.5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remaining approvals rely on permitted alternative sources (e.g., collective bargaining agreements, employer-provided surveys) and are treated separately. Use adjusted approval counts when projecting wage impacts tied to OEWS-based certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for market constraints (visa cap) in impact interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the statutory H-1B numerical cap and strong excess demand (e.g., 781,000 registrations for 85,000 slots in FY2024) mean higher prevailing wages do not necessarily reduce the number of visas granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis distinguishes labor sub-markets and notes that cap constraints can produce allocation effects (e.g., higher-productivity workers receiving visas over lower-productivity ones) and that this interaction may affect transfer quantification; welcomes comment on how DHS rules interact with this proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OEWS-LCA merged dataset and metrics for percent affected
rubrics_metrics.description: LCA and OEWS data for 2020–2024 suggest 22.5% of LCA-certified positions offered wages above the new proposed policy, implying not every employer would be affected; average LCA-offered wage (~$121,908) vs prevailing wage mean (~$111,717) gives an offered-minus-prevailing gap (~$10,191).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use merged dataset metrics (e.g., 'Pct Increase PW' and 'Pct Increase Offered Wage') as proxies for broader impacts when full datasets differ. These proxy metrics help refine estimates of minimum theoretical wage adjustments required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of PERM certifications and immigrant-visa-timed impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not quantify transfer payments associated with many PERM certifications because a portion (about 10%) are for workers not residing in the U.S. who would enter on immigrant visas only after potentially long visa wait times, making immediate wage obligations unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where PERM beneficiaries are already working in the U.S. under temporary visas, their wage impacts are captured in the temporary visa analyses. For immigrant-bound PERM cases, impacts are expected late in the analysis window and are treated as de minimis for quantification purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor demand elasticity assumption for efficiency loss estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a commonly cited average long-run own-wage elasticity of labor demand of −0.3 to estimate how firms adjust labor demand in response to wage increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the elasticity to the average annual percent increase in wage payments (e.g., 6.1% implied average increase) to estimate a potential reduction in labor demand (6.1% * 0.3 ≈ 1.83%), and adjust wage transfer estimates accordingly (e.g., reducing $7.07B to ~$6.94B in example). Acknowledge heterogeneity and uncertainty in elasticity estimates across sectors and occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-quantifiable benefits and potential complementary investments
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify qualitative benefits from higher prevailing wages such as increased retention, training, productivity, attraction of higher-skilled workers, higher rates of patenting, technology diffusion, firm-level productivity growth, and incentives for firms to invest in education and job training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department discusses these benefits qualitatively and requests comments on not-yet-quantified costs (e.g., training program costs, equipment upgrades) that could accompany such benefits. Also notes potential compositional shifts in wage-level shares (more Level III/IV) under DHS lottery and proposed wage changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative approach: Experience Benchmarking with ACS and Mincer equation
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative methodology would benchmark prevailing wage levels to workers with comparable education and experience in the same occupation and geographic area by merging OEWS with ACS microdata and estimating Mincer wage equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate 'potential experience' as age minus years of schooling minus typical school-start-age (often six). Use OEWS 50th/62nd/75th/90th percentiles as base wages, generate ACS-derived ratios (wage premia) comparing expected earnings by education/experience to occupational median, and apply those ratios to OEWS percentiles to produce experience-benchmarked wage levels. Under this alternative, Levels I–IV correspond to 50th, 62nd, 75th, and 90th percentiles among similarly qualified workers, with Level I guaranteeing an alien worker is never paid less than the median native-born worker with comparable credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definitions for Experience Benchmarking Levels I–IV
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Experience Benchmarking: Level I = typical (50th percentile among workers with same occupation, area, education, and experience); Level II = specialized (62nd percentile); Level III = demanding (75th percentile); Level IV = highly demanding (90th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each level is defined relative to workers with the same occupation/area/education/experience combination. Level II–IV reflect progressively higher specialization, expertise, responsibility, or autonomy. The reason for chosen percentiles is to divide the upper half of the distribution relatively evenly; these differ from the proposed OEWS-only percentiles because they incorporate education/experience adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification and regulatory text changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific regulatory amendments proposed include revising §656.40(b) to codify the four-level prevailing wage computation and revising §655.731 to state the Department will use OEWS survey wage data to establish prevailing wages for H-1B, H-1B1, and E-3 classifications, with determinations made by the OFLC NPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains how the statutory formula yields Level II and III from Levels I and IV and instructs that the OFLC Administrator will determine prevailing wages at the four levels; stakeholders should review the proposed regulatory text changes when commenting.
